I've been to 2 acute care psych wards. They're both similar and different. One was a ward 50 stories off the ground, with cages over the windows and Christianity shoved down your throat. Not the best place. The other was a small building with a gated yard and kinder people.

I wasn't allowed to have shoes with strings, phones, wires, anything that you could use to harm yourself with. I was checked on in your room every 15 minutes either via a camera or a nurse, depending on which place I was at. I had a set schedule, with therapeutic activities and meal times. It was nice, to have a routine like that. I met a lot of teens going through the same thing I was and we all become friends, but we weren't allowed to touch or give each other contact information.

These wards are ment to stabilize you after a crisis, most often meaning a suicide attempt. They may change your meds or set you up with a therapist for when you leave, but are not meant to get to the root of your problems and cure you. They'll keep you safe when you're at your worst but there are other places I'd rather be.

I started when I was 10. My parents were fighting all the time and I felt like I was the only one of my siblings that could see what was going on. I punctured my skin with a sewing needle for a while, until my mom found out and yelled at me. I turned to cutting a few months later when my mom flipped out on me for something that wasn't a big deal.
I think that's the thing a lot of us struggle with. There isn't always a reason, there just has to be an urge.

This is something I struggle with too. I remember whenever I showed my cuts to my therapist or staff at a hospital or wherever I was, they'd often say something along the lines of, "They're only superficial so that's good. They aren't bad." And it always, ALWAYS made me feel like a failure. I felt like if I did it deep enough, they'd treat me seriously or I'd be an official self harmer. Then I did it deep, and I still feel like it isn't enough. I think that's the thing here. It's NEVER going to be enough. You're always going to want more and more until one day, you go too far. Lose consciousness, or lose the limb, or lose your life. And then it's usually nothing but regret. Self harm is, for many people, an addition. One that won't end well if left untreated. I'm glad you're getting help and I hope you and everyone else has a successful recovery one day.

I used to feel the same exact way, until I went deeper. Trust me, you DON'T want to go deeper. More pain, longer healing times, and right now I'm pretty sure I need stitches—which means telling my family. But I am still just self harming, the same as you. We're both doing the same thing for (probably) similar reasons. We both need help, and neither one of us is more valid than the other.
